title: The Invisible Power of Trust Between Teammates
author: Admired Leadership
summary: Comparing team trust to invisible physical forces like gravity and magnetism, this piece argues trust is the single biggest differentiator of high-performing teams even though it can't be directly observed. It cites Olympic hockey coach Herb Brooks, who deliberately assembled the 1980 "Miracle on Ice" team from players with a long shared history rather than simply the most talented individuals. The author identifies belief in teammates' competence, more than shared history alone, as the real mechanism behind trust, and recommends leaders create deliberate space for teammates to learn about each other's skills and character.
points: Trust is described as an invisible but decisive factor separating high-performing teams from the rest.
Herb Brooks built the 1980 Olympic hockey team around players with a long shared history rather than pure star talent.
Belief in teammates' competence is identified as the specific mechanism that generates trust.
Leaders are encouraged to create structured opportunities for teammates to learn about each other's skills and character.
quotes: Many of the most profound influences in life are not visible. Think gravity, magnetic fields, friction, and ultrasound.
Of the many qualities that distinguish high-performing teams, trust is the discriminating X-factor by a wide margin.
Instead of selecting college all-stars, Brooks chose players who had played and competed together for years.
If there is a secret to team chemistry, it might be this: trust depends more on what team members think of each other’s skills than on just about anything else.
It wears a cloak but reveals itself in the threads of high performance.
